Step-by-Step Audio Guided Tour: Italian restaurants in the North End, Boston
Tour-Category: restaurant

Stop 1: Pizzeria Regina

Address: 11 1/2 Thacher St, Boston, MA 02113

Coordinates: 42.3631, -71.0542

Type/Specialty: Pizza

Specific Examples: Classic Margherita, Regina's Special, and a variety of toppings.

Orientation: You are about to embark on a walking journey through Italian restaurants in the North End, Boston. As you explore, you will uncover culinary traditions deeply rooted in the stories of immigrants who brought their family recipes across the sea, such as the founding of Pizzeria Regina in 1926 by Luigi D'Auria, a reflection of the Italian heritage that permeates this area. Your first stop is Pizzeria Regina. From Haymarket T Station, head southeast on Blackstone St toward Hanover St, then turn right onto Hanover St. Continue straight for about 0.3 miles, then turn right onto Thacher St. Pizzeria Regina will be on your left. As you walk, you'll notice the vibrant atmosphere of the North End with its charming brick buildings. Stand beneath the old red-and-white neon sign at 11 1/2 Thacher Street—the one that flickers just a little when the front door swings open. The scent that hits you on the sidewalk is unmistakable: hot cheese and tomatoes, edged with a whiff of singed crust. The brickwork is worn, the windows fogged, and if you pause, you’ll catch the shuffle of servers squeezing past the line that coils out the door.

Step inside, and you’re in a place where the kitchen noise is the city’s own heartbeat—pans clanging, orders shouted, and the low hum of a room that’s always hungry. This isn’t just a pizza joint; it’s a slice of North End history, created by the hands of immigrants and kept alive by families who knew how to work a dough and a crowd. Luigi D’Auria started it all in 1926, right here in Boston’s North End. He didn’t just open a restaurant—Pizzeria Regina became a gathering place for the Italian community, a spot to trade stories and recipes, and a place where pizza moved from curiosity to staple. The name he chose, Regina Pizza, meaning “Queen Pizza” in Italian, was no accident. He built something to outlast prohibition and neighborhood shifts, a spot sturdy enough to weather almost a century of change.

Since 1956, the Polcari family has run this place. They took over from Luigi, keeping the oven hot and the tradition alive, even as the North End changed around them. Pizzeria Regina became more than just a restaurant—it’s the original outpost of what is now a New England pizza chain, but this is the flagship, the one that draws lines down Thacher Street every weekend.

There’s no need to book ahead—just bring patience and an appetite. Pizzas here range from $12.50 to $28.25, and the kitchen fires up at 11 a.m. Every day, it closes at 10 p.m. Monday through Saturday, and an hour earlier on Sundays. The focus is pure and simple: Italian pizzas, especially the thin, cheese-laden kind that brings regulars back year after year.

Directions: From Pizzeria Regina, head out onto Thacher Street and stroll towards the bustling Hanover Street. Continue walking along Hanover, passing by the charming shops and cafés that line the street. Bricco will be just a little further down on your right, nestled among the vibrant atmosphere of the North End. Enjoy the sights and sounds as you make your way there! It is about a minute's walk away.

Stop 2: Bricco

Address: 241 Hanover St, Boston, MA 02113

Coordinates: 42.3635, -71.0548

Type/Specialty: Italian Fine Dining

Specific Examples: Homemade pasta, wood-grilled meats, and an extensive wine list.

Orientation: The entrance to Bricco faces the main thoroughfare, but just around the corner, down a narrow cobblestone alley, the lights of Bricco Panetteria flicker late into the night.

Here, Frank DePasquale’s vision fuses the warmth of a southern Italian trattoria with a distinctly modern Boston energy. The scent of baking bread, heavy with olive oil, seeps through the walls—a reminder that just out back, Bricco Panetteria keeps the old-world ritual alive, turning out fresh-baked ciabatta and stuffed loaves late into the evening. Frank DePasquale’s imprint on the neighborhood goes far beyond the plate. The lawsuit pulled local restaurateurs into a public debate about who gets to shape the communal rhythms —whether families could linger over antipasti on the sidewalk, or if the city would restrict the kind of open-air gatherings that define Italian social life here. Bricco is open Monday through Saturday, from 4:00 pm to 11:00 pm, and stays open until 2:00 am on Fridays and Saturdays. Reservations are suggested, and main courses typically range from $38 to $58. The menu offers Italian cuisine with modern interpretations of regional classics—brick oven pizza and beyond. The next stop will carry the scent of simmering sauces, another step in the continuous feast that defines this neighborhood.

Directions: Keep strolling until you reach the intersection with Prince Street, where you’ll find Mamma Maria just a short walk ahead on your left, nestled among the charming brick buildings. Enjoy the sights and sounds of this lovely neighborhood as you make your way!

Stop 3: Mamma Maria

Coordinates: 42.3643, -71.0542

Orientation: This is your vantage for Mamma Maria, just steps away from the bustle of Hanover Street you crossed after leaving Bricco.

Inside Mamma Maria, the atmosphere centers on the details: heavy wooden chairs, crisp linen, candlelight flickering against brick walls. The room’s hush is broken by bursts of laughter from families gathered for a milestone meal — not uncommon here, as locals often choose these tables for birthdays and anniversaries. The emphasis on occasion fits. Mamma Maria is known for hosting North End families across generations, and you’ll often see photographs hanging by the entry of weddings and christenings celebrated in these very rooms. A fact that sets Mamma Maria apart is its focus on handmade pastas and careful sourcing, rooted in owner Jack Antonino’s commitment to the region’s produce. One episode still recounted by staff involves a local grower named Frank, who since the late 1980s has delivered crates of tiny zucchini flowers from a plot in East Boston. According to the kitchen, it was these blossoms that inspired the menu’s signature stuffed fiori — a dish now quietly referenced by other North End menus, but first made here with ricotta whipped by hand and a pinch of mint from Frank’s family garden. The result: a plate whose spring flavor is shaped not by a recipe, but by the relationship between cook and supplier. Mamma Maria’s story also intersects with the broader evolution of Italian dining in Boston, a theme already seen with Bricco’s blend of tradition and innovation. In 2008, during a surge of new Italian-American restaurants, a Boston Globe review called out Mamma Maria’s rabbit pappardelle for honoring “roots without nostalgia,” setting a benchmark for what North End cuisine could become beyond the red sauce staples. Listen now for the sizzle as staff finish that pappardelle with wine in the pan behind the dining room — the sound is a brief bridge between a local past and the ongoing conversation about what Italian-American food means in Boston. The lingering taste of their legendary tiramisu will leave you contemplating the sweet journey we’ve taken.

Together, these stops highlight the rich tapestry of Italian culinary tradition and innovation in Boston's North End, showcasing how family legacies and local ingredients shape the dining experience. This journey reminds us that each meal is not just about food, but also about the stories and connections that bring communities together. That's 3 stops in all.
